claims.quote: While seasonal influenza (flu) viruses are detected year-round in the United States, influenza viruses typically circulate during the fall and winter during what's known as the flu season.

claims.text: February is the most common peak month: 17 seasons, then December 7, January 6, March 6; some seasons peak in December, others in February or March; peak month varies (peak section, chart, timing, FAQ).

claims.text: Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine every season, with rare exceptions (key takeaways, who section, citable summary).
claims.quote: Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine every season with rare exceptions.

claims.text: Ideally everyone should be vaccinated by the end of October; September and October are generally good times (key takeaways, timing, FAQ).
claims.quote: September and October are generally good times to be vaccinated against influenza. ... Ideally, everyone should be vaccinated by the end of October.

claims.text: It takes about two weeks after vaccination for protective antibodies to develop (peak and too-late sections).
claims.quote: It takes about two weeks after vaccination for antibodies that protect against flu to develop in the body.

claims.text: Most adults should not get vaccinated early, in July or August, because protection may decrease over time (effectiveness section).
claims.quote: Most adults, especially those 65 years and older, and pregnant women in the first or second trimester should generally not get vaccinated early (in July or August) because protection may decrease over time.

claims.text: In adults 65 and older, flu complications, hospitalizations and deaths are generally most common; three vaccines (high-dose, adjuvanted, recombinant) are preferentially recommended (risk table).
claims.quote: complications, hospitalizations, and deaths due to influenza are generally most common among people 65 years and older. ... For adults 65 years and older, there are 3 flu vaccines that are preferentially recommended.

claims.text: Children younger than 6 months are too young to get a flu shot (risk table).
claims.quote: Children younger than 6 months of age are too young to get a flu shot.

claims.text: Vaccination in the third trimester can help protect infants for the first few months after birth (risk table, FAQ).
claims.quote: Vaccination during July and August also can be considered for mothers who are in the third trimester of pregnancy, because this can help protect their infants for the first few months after birth

claims.text: If pregnant, get a flu shot and not the nasal spray vaccine (FAQ).
claims.quote: If you are pregnant or have certain chronic health conditions, you should get a flu shot. ... Also, if you are pregnant, you should not get the nasal spray flu vaccine.

claims.text: Health care personnel and household contacts and caregivers of people with risk-raising conditions are listed among groups to vaccinate first when supply is limited (risk table).
claims.quote: When vaccine supply is limited, vaccination efforts should focus on delivering vaccination to the following people ... Health care personnel ... Household contacts and caregivers of people with medical conditions that put them at increased risk

claims.text: People with egg allergy may get any flu vaccine, egg-based or not, that is otherwise appropriate for their age and health (who section).
claims.quote: People with egg allergy may get any vaccine (egg-based or non-egg-based) that is otherwise appropriate for their age and health status.
